lemma: Bounded-support reduction for THR o THR #SAT, exact for all integer weights. Let f(x) = [sum_j v_j [W_j.x >= t_j] >= T], supp(j) = {i : W_ji != 0}, V2 = union of supp(j) over gates with |supp(j)| >= 2, V1 = (union of supp(j) over unary gates) minus V2, V0 = [n] minus (V1 union V2). Then #f = 2^{|V0|} * sum over y in {0,1}^{V2} of N(y), where N(y) = #{z in {0,1}^{V1} : sum_i a_i z_i >= T - S(y) - c}, a_i = sum over unary gates j on i of v_j (b1_j - b0_j), c = sum over unary gates of v_j b0_j, S(y) = sum over gates with supp in V2 of v_j [W_j.y >= t_j], and b0_j, b1_j are the values of the unary gate at x_i = 0, 1.
gap: G0001 stays OPEN; this lemma closes no obligation. The saving is 2^{|V0| + |V1|/2}, which is 2^{(1-delta)n} only when |V0| + |V1|/2 >= delta n. In that regime the instance has delta n variables that are dummies (V0) or occur only in single-variable gates (V1). Dummies are removed by preprocessing, and the V1 case is a linear count in z, so the regime is not a nontrivial subclass in the G0001 sense. The worst case V2 = [n] gives zero saving (cubic incidence: cm-75ca9a8632b746a8). Repair target unchanged: a subclass with every variable in a gate of support >= 2 and running time 2^{(1-delta)n} poly, proved (G0002 pathwidth or G0007 restriction lemma).
proved_step: PROOF. Every gate is either supported in V2 (all gates with |supp| >= 2, and unary gates on V2) or a unary gate on a variable of V1; no unary gate sits on V0. A unary gate on i equals b0 + (b1 - b0) x_i with b1 - b0 in {-1,0,1}, so the top sum equals S(y) + c + sum_i a_i z_i, where y is the V2 part and z the V1 part of x. The indicator of f therefore depends only on (y,z), and the V0 bits are free, which gives the displayed formula. Algorithm: precompute once the sorted subset-sum lists of the two halves of V1 (2^{|V1|/2} entries each, O(2^{|V1|/2} poly) time). For each y (2^{|V2|} values), compute S(y) in poly(n,m) time and count pairs (l, r) with l + r >= theta(y) by a two-pointer pass over the sorted lists in O(2^{|V1|/2}) time. Total time poly(n,m) * 2^{|V2| + |V1|/2} = poly(n,m) * 2^{n - |V0| - |V1|/2}. Correctness holds for all integer weights because the formula is exact. Measured: thr2_evaluate cm-dfa09e24096b46f8 (70 tests, public, held-out and adversarial, wrong = []), with speedup below 1 for n <= 16.

proved_step: Bandwidth DP for THR o THR #SAT. Setting: variables 1..n in a FIXED order that is part of the input. Bottom gate j has integer weights W_j with support S_j (nonempty), last(j) = max S_j, window L_j = max S_j - min S_j + 1. Top gate: integer v_j, integer T, f(x) = [sum_j v_j [W_j.x >= t_j] >= T]. Let l = max_j L_j and V = sum_j |v_j|. Claim: #f = #{x in {0,1}^n : f(x)=1} is computed exactly in time O(n^2 m 2^(l-1) (2V+1)). Proof: process i = 1..n. Frontier F_i = {u <= i : u in S_j for some j with last(j) > i}. Claim |F_i| <= l-1. If u in F_i via gate j, then u >= min S_j = last(j) - L_j + 1 >= i+2-l, so F_i lies in [i+2-l, i], a set of size at most l-1. DP state after step i: (assignment to F_i, partial top sum P over gates with last(j) <= i), with the count of prefixes x_1..x_i producing it. Transition by choosing x_{i+1}: a gate with last(j) = i+1 reads only coordinates u in S_j with u <= i (which lie in F_i, since last(j) > i) and u = i+1, so its value is determined by the state and x_{i+1}; add its weighted value to P; keep F_{i+1}. Final answer = sum of counts over states with P >= T. Number of states at most 2^(l-1) (2V+1), since P lies in [-V, V]. Correctness follows by induction on i.

evidence: Independent review (not the author). Hand proof: (1) every gate with |supp|>=2 has supp inside V2; a unary gate whose variable lies in V1 is the only kind removed from A; unary gates on V2 variables stay in A and are evaluated from y, so A-gates depend only on y. (2) Variables in V0 occur in no gate, so f does not depend on them, giving the factor 2^|V0|. (3) For fixed y, each V1 unary gate j on i contributes v_j[b0_j + (b1_j - b0_j) z_i]; summing over gates on i gives the linear form c + S(y) + sum_i a_i z_i with a_i as stated, so N(y) is exactly the count in the lemma. Summing over y gives the identity. Exact check: cm-d9302cb74f964ac1 (400 random THR o THR instances, n in 3..9, m in 2..8, 0 mismatches, instances with V1 nonempty 128, max |V2| 8). proved_step: SUB-V2 (exact algorithm and running time, for all integer THR o THR). Let f(x) = [sum_j v_j [W_j.x >= t_j] >= T] with m gates over n variables, all |W_ji|, |t_j|, |v_j| <= B. Let V2 = union of supp(j) over gates with |supp(j)| >= 2, and l = |V2|. Let V1 = (union of supp(j) over unary gates) minus V2, k = |V1|, V0 = [n] minus (V1 union V2). Algorithm: (a) for each unary gate on i in V1 set a_i += v_j (b1_j - b0_j), c += v_j b0_j, where b0_j = [0 >= t_j], b1_j = [W_ji >= t_j]; (b) let A be the remaining gates; for each y in {0,1}^{V2} compute S(y) = sum over A of v_j [W_j.y >= t_j] (A-gates have support inside V2, see the identity); (c) compute the distribution of sum_i a_i z_i over z in {0,1}^{V1} by an integer DP of range at most 4nmB+1; (d) output 2^{|V0|} * sum_y #{z : sum a_i z_i >= T - c - S(y)}. Correctness: the identity of S0007 (SURVIVED_REVIEW). Time: O(2^l (mn + n^2 m B)) arithmetic operations plus O(nmB) precomputation. Consequence (SUBCLASS C_delta): instances with |V2| <= (1-delta) n, any m = poly(n), weights bounded by poly(n), are counted in time 2^{(1-delta) n} poly(n,m,B) with NO variable ordering needed (V2 is computed directly). Exact for all instances: general time 2^{|V2|} poly <= 2^n poly. Scope: this is a constant-base saving on a subclass, not 2^n / n^{omega(1)}, and it does not close G0001 in general (the general class can have V2 = [n]). Open for the next step: a subclass where |V2| is small but m is n^alpha and the supports are unbounded in count, or an enrichment where the 2^{l} enumeration is replaced by a DP over the V2 supports (pathwidth of the V2 gate hypergraph, G0002). Authored by R1075; not reviewed by its author.

lemma: LEMMA IW (windowed interval DP, exact for all integer weights). Setting: integers k>=1, D>=1, B>=0, n>=k. Bottom gates g_j(x) = [sum_{i=0}^{k-1} w_{j,i} x_{a_j+i} >= t_j] with 0 <= a_j <= n-k, |w_{j,i}| <= B, at most D gates per start a. Top f(x) = [sum_j v_j g_j(x) >= T], S = sum_j |v_j|. Then |f^{-1}(1)| is computed by a left-to-right DP over positions p = 0..n-1. State after reading x_0..x_{p-1}: key (c, (tau_j)_{j in A_p}), where c is the sum of v_j g_j over completed gates, A_p = gates with p-k+1 <= a_j <= p-1, and tau_j = clamp(t_j minus the read part of gate j, L_j, U_j+1), with [L_j,U_j] the range of the unread part of gate j's sum. Proof: (1) clamping preserves gate values; (2) the future depends only on the key, so equal keys can be merged; (3) U_j-L_j <= 2Bk, so tau_j takes <= 2Bk+2 values; c lies in an interval of S+1 integers; |A_p| <= D(k-1); so each level has <= (S+1)(2Bk+2)^{D(k-1)} keys; (4) each key has 2 transitions with O(Dk) updates, total O(n Dk^2 (S+1)(2Bk+2)^{D(k-1)}) integer operations. Scope: D = O(1) gives m = O(n) bottom gates, and k = n/log^2 n gives 2^{O(n/log n)} poly(n) time. This does NOT reach m = n^alpha (alpha>1), where D ~ n^{alpha-1} makes (2Bk+2)^{Dk} exceed 2^{o(n)}. proved_step: LEMMA-RO (random-order frontier DP, Las Vegas). Setting: fixed integers c,k >= 1; D = c(k-1); THR o THR circuit f = [sum_j v_j g_j >= T] with bottom gates g_j = [sum_{i in S_j} w_{ji} x_i >= t_j], |S_j| <= k, each variable in at most c supports S_j, |v_j|, |w_{ji}| at most V(n) polynomial, any number m of gates. Let beta_D = (D/(D+1)) (D+1)^{-1/D} < 1. Claim: for every eps > 0 there is a Las Vegas algorithm computing #f exactly with expected time poly(n,m,V) 2^{(beta_D+eps) n}. Proof: (1) Fix an ordering pi of variables, pos(i) its position. Gate j completes at ct_j = max pos over S_j. K_t = {i : pos(i) <= t and some gate containing i completes after t}. A DP over x restricted to K_t plus the partial sum (range at most 2mV+1 values) is exact, because variables outside K_t are no longer read by any unfinished gate. State count at most 2^{|K_t|}(2mV+1). (2) i is in K_t iff pos(i) <= t and some u in N(i) has pos(u) > t, where N(i) is the union of S_j minus i over gates containing i; |N(i)| <= D. With s = |N(i)|+1 <= D+1 and tau = t/n: P(i in K_t) = P(pos(i) <= t) - P(all of {i} union N(i) in the prefix) <= tau - C(t,s)/C(n,s) <= tau - tau^{D+1} + O(D^2/n). Maximising over tau gives E|K_t| <= beta_D n + O(D^2). (3) A transposition of two positions changes the membership of at most 2(D+1) variables, so |K_t| is 2(D+1)-Lipschitz for transpositions. A Maurey/McDiarmid-type bound for uniform permutations gives deviation eps n with probability 1 - exp(-Omega(eps^2 n / D^2)); a union bound over t <= n gives, for large n, max_t |K_t| <= (beta_D+eps) n + O(D^2) with probability at least 1/2. (4) Algorithm: sample pi, compute max_t |K_t| exactly (poly time), accept if below the threshold, otherwise resample. Expected at most 2 trials; then run the DP. The output is exact; only the running time is random. Consequence: for fixed c,k, the subclass admits a counting algorithm with running time 2^{(beta_D+eps) n} poly(n,m,V), which is a strict 2^{(1-delta)n} saving with delta = 1 - beta_D - eps > 0 for any number of gates m, including m = n^alpha. The non-literal part has at most cn/2 gates by LEMMA-OVL.

lemma: Let W in Z^{m x n}, t in Z^m, and let G(x) = ([w_j . x >= t_j])_j for x in {0,1}^n. Then the number of distinct rows of the 2^n x m matrix G is at most min(2^m, sum_{i=0}^{n} C(m,i)). Proof: (a) 2^m is trivial. (b) Replace t_j by t_j - 1/2. Since w_j . x - t_j is an integer, [w_j . x >= t_j] = [w_j . x > t_j - 1/2], so every cube point lies strictly off each shifted hyperplane. Each row is therefore the sign vector of a region of the arrangement of m affine hyperplanes in R^n, and such an arrangement has at most sum_{i<=n} C(m,i) regions (Buck / Zaslavsky). Scope: integer data, any m, n. This is a bound on patterns only.
gap: Does NOT close G0001 or G0002: it bounds the pattern count, not the cost of enumerating realised patterns. Realised patterns cannot be enumerated from the region bound, because deciding whether a region contains a 0/1 point is hard extraction. For m = n^alpha with alpha > 1 the bound sum_{i<=n} C(m,i) >= 2^n, so it gives no saving.

proved_step: S0040 (CLAIMED, unreviewed). Setting: f(x) = #{x in {0,1}^n : sum_j v_j [<w_{idx(j)}, x> >= t_j] >= T} for m bottom gates whose weight vectors take at most d distinct values w^(1..d) in Z^n with |w^(k)_i| <= B; t_j, v_j, T arbitrary integers. Claim: f is computed exactly in O(n (2Bn+1)^d (m d + 1)) arithmetic operations. Proof: DP over prefixes. For level i let z_k = <w^(k)_{<=i}, x_{<=i}> for k = 1..d; the state is z in Z^d. Since |z_k| <= B i <= Bn, there are at most (2Bn+1)^d states per level. The transition from level i-1 to i adds b * w^(k)_i to each z_k for b in {0,1}, so the count table at level i is a function of the table at level i-1. Each gate value [<w_{idx(j)},x> >= t_j] is a function of the final z alone, so f = sum over final states z with sum_j v_j [z_{idx(j)} >= t_j] >= T of their counts. Correctness is by induction on i. Scope: polynomial time when d is constant and B is polynomial in n. GAP: this does not close G0001. General THR o THR needs d = Theta(m) (the measured thr2 family, cm-c77b7124cbc643ef, has about one form per gate), and the bound is exponential there. It is a standard, self-made subclass bound; it counts as progress only after review with confirms_closure, and it is not progress by itself.

The junta observation is mathematically correct: U is the union of supports of all bottom weight vectors, so for each j, W_j has zeros outside U, hence W_j.x = W_j|_U . x_U. Thus f(x) depends only on the s variables in U. The n-s variables outside U are free, contributing factor 2^(n-s). Enumerating all 2^s assignments to U, evaluating m gates (each O(s) time), and counting satisfying assignments takes O(2^s * m * s) time. The final multiplication by 2^(n-s) is O(1) arithmetic. This is a correct exact algorithm for the junta subclass (s relevant variables). The claim's self-noted caveat that it gives 2^n poly for full-support gates (s=n) and does not close G0001 is accurate. No counterexample exists; the step is a valid ALGORITHM for the stated subclass.

The LEMMA-DIR algorithm is mathematically correct. It computes #SAT for THR o THR circuits with at most D distinct weight vectors (directions) with bounded entries. The dynamic programming over the D-dimensional projection Y(x) = (a_1.x, ..., a_D.x) is exact: N^(i)_y counts prefixes with partial sums y, and the support stays in the box [-iB, iB]^D of size at most (2iB+1)^D. The recursion N^(i)_y = N^(i-1)_y + N^(i-1)_{y - c_i} (with c_i = (a_{1,i},...,a_{D,i})) is correct because x_i in {0,1}. Final sum over states evaluates g(y) = sum_j v_j [y_{d(j)} >= t_j] and sums N_n(y) * [g(y) >= T]. Total operations O(n * (2Bn+1)^D * (D+m)). The corollary condition D <= (1-delta)n/log2(2Bn+1) gives running time 2^{(1-delta)n} poly(n). This is a valid ALGORITHM for the stated subclass (few distinct directions). It does not cover D=Theta(n) and does not close G0001 for the general case, as correctly noted. No counterexample exists.

Verified by exhaustive testing on random instances (n=8, D=3, m=6, 10 tests) and edge cases (D=1, zero weights, negative weights). The dynamic programming over the D-dimensional projection Y(x) = (<d_1,x>,...,<d_D,x>) is mathematically correct: each variable x_i contributes either 0 or the i-th coordinates of all D direction vectors, so the recursion N_i(s) = N_{i-1}(s) + N_{i-1}(s - c_i) where c_i = (d_{1,i},...,d_{D,i}) exactly counts prefixes. The state space is bounded by [-nB, nB]^D, giving at most (2nB+1)^D states. Each step does O(D) work per state, and evaluating F(s) costs O(m). Total time O(n * (2nB+1)^D * (D + m)). This matches the claimed bound. The algorithm is exact for the stated subclass (few distinct directions). No counterexample found. The step is a standard counting argument (not novel), but it is correct and survives review.

The DP construction is mathematically correct for the stated subclass. State = (last L-1 bits, partial sum s in [-mV, mV]). At position i, the window of length L contains x_{a_j..i} for every gate j with interval I_j ending at i (since l_j <= L). Each assignment x maps to exactly one DP path. Gate evaluation depends only on x restricted to I_j, which is in the window when the gate is processed. Final sum over states with s >= T equals #f exactly. Time complexity O(n m^2 L V 2^L) is correctly derived. The lemma correctly identifies its scope: interval supports in one fixed order only. It does NOT close G0002 (which requires pw <= (1-delta)n for a subclass of size n^alpha with alpha > 1), because interval supports of length L allow at most n distinct intervals, so m <= n (alpha <= 1). The path-decomposition DP is mathematically correct. The clipping lemma is mathematically correct. For fixed x_A, the condition W_j x >= t_j becomes W^B_j x_B >= t_j - W^A_j x_A. Since W^B_j x_B is bounded in [lo_j, hi_j], values below lo_j are always true (clip to lo_j), values above hi_j are always false (clip to hi_j+1 as impossible threshold). The condition depends on x_A only through the clipped threshold c(x_A). Summing over c gives exact count. K_clip bound: each c_j takes at most |supp_B(j)| + 2 values because the clipped threshold ranges over the |supp_B(j)| + 1 possible values of W^B_j x_B plus one 'impossible' value. This is sound. The lemma does not yet close any obligation; it's a building block.

No counterexample found; the proof is complete for the stated subclass (circuits where most gates concentrate on a delta*n core B). The lemma analyzes Pr[M_k nonconstant] under a random restriction keeping each variable free with probability p. For unit-weight majority with threshold t = floor((k+1)/2), the gate becomes constant iff the number of free variables f = Bin(k,p) satisfies that all completions of the fixed bits give the same output. This happens unless the fixed 1s count is in [t-f, t-1] (for f free variables). The probability is sum_f P(Bin(k,p)=f) * P(t-f <= Bin(k-f,1/2) <= t-1). The window has f points, and max_j P(Bin(m,1/2)=j) <= sqrt(2/(pi m))(1+o(1)). So Pr <= E[f] * sqrt(2/(pi(k-f))) = sqrt(2/pi) p sqrt(k) (1+o(1)) + tail. Asymptotic sharpness as p sqrt(k) -> 0: only f=1 contributes at first order, giving Pr ~ p k * sqrt(2/(pi(k-1))) ~ sqrt(2/pi) p sqrt(k). The tail for f > k/2 is exponentially small by Chernoff. The proof sketch is correct for unit weights; the general-weight case (Littlewood-Offord) is correctly noted as open. The tail term proof is sketched but the bound holds. No counterexample found for the unit-weight case.

The proof correctly decomposes Pr[nonconstant] = sum_f P(F=f) * W_f where F ~ Bin(k,p) is the number of free variables and W_f = Pr[nonconstant | F=f]. Given f free variables, the fixed part has m = k-f variables with sum s ~ Bin(m,1/2). The gate is nonconstant iff s is in the window [t-f, t-1] of size f, so W_f <= f * max_j P(Bin(m,1/2)=j). The max-pmf bound max_j P(Bin(m,1/2)=j) <= sqrt(2/(pi(m-1))) for m >= 2 is standard (central binomial coefficient estimate). For f <= k/2, m >= k/2 gives m-1 >= (k-2)/2, so W_f <= 2f/sqrt(pi(k-2)). Summing with E[F] = kp yields the first term (2/sqrt(pi)) sqrt(k/(k-2)) p sqrt(k). For f > k/2, the sum is bounded by P(F >= k/2). The Chernoff bound with e^lambda = (1-p)/p gives P(F >= k/2) <= (2 sqrt(p(1-p)))^k <= (4p)^{k/2} for p <= 1/4 (trivial for p > 1/4). The finite check cm-ead2ddafe1824903 (558 cases, k=4..59 and 64..1024, p in [1e-4, 0.25]) found 0 violations of either the window bound or the total bound, worst ratio 0.71. The proof is correct for unit-weight majority; the general-weight case (Littlewood-Offord) is correctly noted as open. No counterexample or argument gap found.

The proof correctly applies the Erdos-Sperner (Littlewood-Offord) theorem: for integers a_i with |a_i| >= 1, any open interval of length 2 contains at most C(r, floor(r/2)) of the 2^r subset sums. Here c = sum_{i in F} U_i x_i with x_i in {0,1}, r = |F|, and U_i = W_ji for non-zero weights (|U_i| >= 1 since weights are integers). The gate is non-constant iff c lies in the integer interval [t_j - hi, t_j - lo - 1] of size L = hi - lo <= sum_F |U_i| <= Bk. For each integer s in this interval, the open interval (s-1, s+1) has length 2, so by Erdos-Sperner, at most C(r, floor(r/2)) subset sums fall into it. Thus Pr[c = s] <= C(r, floor(r/2))/2^r. Union bound over L values gives Pr[non-constant | F] <= L * C(r, floor(r/2))/2^r. The bound C(r, floor(r/2))/2^r <= 1/sqrt(r) for r >= 1 is standard (central binomial coefficient). The earlier window-of-length-2 version was correctly refuted (cm-11329b5046ac4967: 24 violations); the point version fixes this by using intervals of length 2 around each integer. The finite check cm-0fc2b38402284a21 (300 instances, worst ratio 1.0) corroborates the point version. No counterexample or argument gap found for this proof.

The algorithm correctly reduces #SAT for THR o THR with top fan-in <= 2 to 2-D orthogonal dominance counting. With |supp v| <= 2, we have at most 2 gates with non-zero top weights. For each pattern b in {0,1}^2 with v.b >= T, the conditions g_j(x)=b_j are inequalities on the sums W_j.x. Splitting x = (x_A, x_B) with |x_A| = floor(n/2), each inequality becomes P_b(x_B) >= Q_b(x_A) or Q_b(x_A) >= P_b(x_B) in Z, which is a 2-D dominance problem. Counting pairs (x_A, x_B) with P_b(x_B) >= Q_b(x_A) for all such patterns is an offline 2-D dominance count, solvable by sorting and Fenwick tree in O(N log N) = O(2^{n/2} n) time per pattern. There are at most 4 patterns, so total time O(2^{n/2} n log(2^{n/2})). The finite check cm-6b6e6034b4cb44d9 (120 instances, n in {6,8,10,12} plus scale checks at 14,16) found 0 mismatches vs brute force. The scope is correctly limited to constant top fan-in 2; general unbounded top fan-in (O1) and lower-bound transfers are not claimed. No counterexample or argument gap found.

Splitting x = (x_A, x_B) with |x_A| = floor(n/2), each inequality becomes P_b(x_B) >= Q_b(x_A) or the reverse in Z^k, which is a k-dimensional orthogonal dominance counting problem. For fixed b, this is an offline k-dimensional dominance count between N_B = 2^{ceil(n/2)} points and N_A = 2^{floor(n/2)} queries, solvable with a k-dimensional range tree in O(N log^{k-1} N) time. This is a basic counting argument (double counting / pigeonhole principle). Let C be a THR o THR circuit with m bottom gates g_j = [W_j·x ≥ t_j]. After removing constant gates (always-true gates whose v_j is folded into T, always-false gates dropped), we have m' remaining gates with nonempty supports N_j ⊆ {1,...,n}. Let d_i = |{j : i ∈ N_j}| be the degree of variable i (number of gates it participates in). The sum of degrees ∑_i d_i equals ∑_j |N_j| (each occurrence of a variable in a gate is counted exactly once on each side). Since each remaining gate has nonempty support, |N_j| ≥ 1, so ∑_j |N_j| ≥ m'. Therefore ∑_i d_i ≥ m'. If every d_i ≤ c, then ∑_i d_i ≤ c·n, giving m' ≤ c·n. For m' = n^α with α > 1, if all d_i ≤ c then n^α ≤ c·n, so n^(α-1) ≤ c, meaning some variable has degree at least n^(α-1) (otherwise the sum would be < n^α). The argument is elementary, correct, and its scope is clearly stated. No counterexample or gap exists.

The cut-crossing DP is a standard dynamic programming approach for THR o THR circuits. K(C) is the maximum number of gates that cross any cut in the variable order (gates with non-zero weights on both sides of the cut). The DP processes variables left-to-right, maintaining for each gate crossing the current cut its partial sum s_j = ∑_{l < i} W_jl x_l. Each partial sum lies in [-Bn, Bn], giving at most (2Bn+1)^K states. The top threshold T is tracked by accumulating v_j for gates that become decided (always 1) and accounting for the rest at the end; V = ∑|v_j| bounds the range of accumulated top weights. The transition at each variable is exact because gate outcomes depend additively on the prefix. The time bound O(n m K (2Bn+1)^K (V+1)) is correct for this DP. The consequence for K(C) ≤ (1-δ)n/log₂(2Bn+1) giving 2^((1-δ)n) poly(n) time follows by substituting the bound on K. The scope is correctly limited to circuits with small cut-crossing number K; generic THR o THR circuits have K = Θ(m) which is typically much larger. No counterexample or argument gap found.

The S-RANK-r lemma is correct. The weight matrix W (m x n over Q) has rank r. Pick r linearly independent rows Bm (basis). Each row W_j = c_j Bm with exact rational coefficients c_j, so W_j.x = c_j.s(x) where s(x) = Bm x in Z^r. The DP maintains the count of prefixes reaching each state s_p in [-Bp, Bp]^r, with at most (2Bn+1)^r states per level. Transition: s_{p+1} = s_p + Bm[:, p+1] * x_{p+1}. After all n variables, gate j's value is [c_j.s_n >= t_j] (exact rational comparison). The top gate sum is sum_j v_j * gate_j. Sum counts for states where sum >= T. Time: O(n * (2Bn+1)^r * poly(m,n,r)) for DP transitions plus O((2Bn+1)^r * m) for final evaluation. The cited experiments cm-a8ea3bacdc574c44 (72 instances, 0 mismatches) and cm-3b8036f363ce479a (54 instances with exact rational arithmetic, 0 mismatches) independently verify the algorithm on concrete instances. No argument gap or counterexample found. Scope correctly limited to integer weights bounded by B, rational thresholds, rank r of W over Q. Does not close G0001/G0002 as stated.

The Windowed cut DP (S0106) is a correct refinement of the cut-crossing DP (S0100). The key insight is tracking only UNDecided gates at each cut i, where a gate is decided if its partial sum s_j plus the minimum/maximum possible future contribution already determines its output. The invariant holds: decided gates have fixed outcomes for all completions, so their top weights v_j can be folded into tau immediately. Undecided gates' outcomes depend additively on s_j and the suffix, so transitions are exact. The state space is bounded by (2Bn+1)^U * (sum|v|+1) where U = max_i undecided_started(i). Since U <= K (cut-crossing number), this strictly improves S0100's (2Bn+1)^K bound when some crossing gates become decided early. No argument gap or counterexample found. The algorithm correctly computes exact #SAT. Does not close G0001/G0002 as stated.

The LEMMA IS-COVER (S0114) is correct for its stated scope. The proof uses standard independent-set conditioning: an independent set I of size >= n/(Delta+1) exists by the greedy argument. Fixing x_C decouples the variables in I because each support S is a clique (so |S cap I| <= 1). For each fixed x_C, the function F(x) = c(x_C) + sum_{u in I} phi_u(y_u) where y = x_I and phi_u depends only on y_u. Counting y with sum phi_u(y_u) >= T - c(x_C) is a subset-sum DP over I with O(|I| V) states, V = sum_S max|h_S|. Total time 2^{|C|} * O(|I| V + m 2^k) = 2^{n-|I|} poly = 2^{(1-delta)n} poly with delta = 1/(Delta+1). The scope is exactly: fan-in <= k (constant), co-occurrence degree <= Delta (constant), any m = n^alpha bottom gates, polynomial integer weights. This is a special case of G0001 (bounded fan-in) with the extra hypothesis Delta = O(1). It does NOT close G0001, G0002, G0005, G0007 as stated, because dense overlap (Delta = Theta(n)) gives delta -> 0. The argument is a known technique (bounded-degree counting / independent set conditioning), so it may be judged trivial under the owner's progress criterion. No argument gap or counterexample found.

The lemma is correct for its stated subclass. The hypothesis partitions variables outside S into private sets P_j (disjoint across gates) plus free variables F. For each fixed assignment a to the s shared variables, each bottom gate j has a fixed base contribution from S. The number of assignments to its private variables P_j making the gate output 1 (c_j[1]) or 0 (c_j[0]) is computed exactly by a subset-sum DP over P_j in time O(|P_j| V_j). Since P_j are disjoint, the gates' outputs are independent given a. The top threshold gate's sum is a convolution of independent two-point distributions (v_j with multiplicity c_j[1], 0 with c_j[0]), computed by a DP over total top sum (table size <= V+1 = sum |v_j| + 1). Summing over all 2^s assignments to S and multiplying by 2^{|F|} for free variables gives the exact #SAT. Running time: 2^s * (sum_j O(|P_j| V_j) + O(m V)) = O(2^s * m * n * V). The exhaustive check cm-b5d9ef4c88e14bb6 (20 random instances, n in {8,10,12}, m in {4,6,8}, s in {0..5}, B in {3,5,20}) confirms exact counts match brute force. This is a non-trivial exact algorithm for a stated subclass, meeting the intermediate goal of a proved speed-up for a restricted subclass (O2 in THR-SAT obligation). It does not yet reach the full obligation G0001 (bounded fan-in) because the subclass requires the disjointness structure outside S, but it is valid progress.

The low-rank weight algorithm (S0127) is correct for its stated subclass. The proof correctly reduces the problem to counting solutions by the r-dimensional vector s(x) = Bx where B consists of r independent rows of the weight matrix W. Since each row W_j = C_j B, the bottom gate outputs depend only on s(x). The DP computes H_n(sigma) = #{x: Bx = sigma} over the box Q of possible partial sums, where each coordinate lies in an interval of length at most beta n. The box has at most (beta n + 1)^r points. Each of the n steps updates O(r) values per point, giving O(n (beta n + 1)^r) for the DP. The final sum evaluates g(sigma) = sum v_j [C_j.sigma >= t_j] at each sigma in Q, taking O(m r) per point. Total time O((beta n + 1)^r (n + m r)). This is a non-trivial exact algorithm for the low-rank weight subclass (O2 in THR-SAT obligation). If r <= (1-delta)n/log2(beta n) the exponent beats 2^n. No argument gap or counterexample found.

The proof attempt only shows E[# non-constant gates] <= p * Delta * n via union bound Pr[gate j non-constant] <= p |S_j|. The bandwidth DP (S0131) is correct for its stated subclass B_k where all bottom gate supports are intervals of length at most k in some variable order. The proof uses the standard windowing technique: F_i (the frontier of variables at position i that share a support with some variable > i) has size at most k-1 because any such variable u must satisfy u >= i-k+2. The state is (y, s) where y = x restricted to F_i and s is the partial top sum. There are at most 2^{k-1} * (2V+1) states per level. Transitions for each x_i value update gates whose maximum support element is i, then compute the new frontier F_i. Each transition takes O(|F_i| + number of gates ending at i) = O(k + m_i) time. Summed over n steps this gives O(2^k * (n + m k) * V). This is a non-trivial exact algorithm for the interval support subclass (O2 in THR-SAT obligation). It does not close the general bounded fan-in obligation G0001 because interval supports are a proper subset of bounded fan-in supports. No argument gap found.

The decomposition #f = sum_K mu(K) N(K) is exact. The bound hi_j - lo_j + 2 = sum_i |B_ji| + 2 <= s n^b + 2 <= n^(b+1) + 2; for n >= 8 this is <= 2 * n^(b+1). So |K*| <= (2 n^(b+1))^m = 2^(m + m(b+1) log2 n) <= 2^(n/4 + n/4) = 2^(n/2) using m <= n/(4(b+1) log2 n). Analyzed the WINDOW LEMMA claims (a)-(d) for class C(n,k,D) where each row has support exactly a block of k consecutive positions in some unknown order pi*, at most D rows per block. Claim (a): nu(sigma) <= Dk for any C1P ordering sigma. Proof: at position p, intervals of length k containing p have left endpoints in [p-k+1, p] (exactly k intervals); each exact interval has <= D rows by class definition. So at most Dk rows cover p. Correct. Claim (b): PQ-tree finds a C1P ordering in linear time (Booth-Lueker 1976); pi* is a C1P ordering so one exists. Correct. Claim (c): DP over positions with state = (sum of v over decided gates, partial sums of open gates). Gate decided at its last support position. Partial sum of open gate in [-Bk, Bk] (k nonzeros, each |W_ji|<=B). Number of open gates = nu(sigma) <= Dk. State count <= (2Vm+1)(2Bk+1)^{Dk}. Transition updates partial sums for gates containing next position, moves gates whose last position is reached to decided sum. Correct. Claim (d): With m <= Dn, k <= c n/(D log2 n), c<1: exponent Dk log2(2Bk+1) = (c n/log2 n) * log2(Theta(n/log n)) = (c+o(1))n. Running time poly(n) 2^{(c+o(1))n}, speed-up over 2^n for c<1. Correct for the stated class. Gaps acknowledged in the step: (i) exact windows only (no internal zeros), (ii) multiplicity D essential, (iii) needs independent review (this review), (iv) not a speed-up for general THR o THR. No error found in the mathematical reasoning for the restricted class C(n,k,D).

The DP construction is standard for threshold circuits with bounded integer weights. The residual r_j = t_j - sum_{l=1..i} w_jl x_l tracks how much more weight is needed to reach threshold t_j. The maximum possible remaining contribution from variables i+1..n is at most sum_{l=i+1..n} |w_jl| <= B(n-i), and the minimum is at least -B(n-i). Thus: gate is decided TRUE iff r_j <= -B(n-i) (even minimum remaining contribution suffices), decided FALSE iff r_j > B(n-i) (even maximum remaining contribution insufficient), otherwise undecided with r_j in (-B(n-i), B(n-i)] which contains exactly 2B(n-i) integer values. Adding the two decided states gives at most 2B(n-i)+2 <= 2Bn+2 states per gate. The product over k gates gives at most (2Bn+2)^k state vectors. Transitions take poly(k) time per state per variable. The bound (2Bn+2)^k corrects the earlier (Bn+1)^k which omitted the negative residual range. Verified by hand on n=2, k=1, B=1 example: gate [x1+x2>=1] with t=1. DP states at i=0: r in {-1,0,1,2} plus decided-T/F = 6 = 2Bn+2. Transitions yield correct count 3. No counterexample found; argument is sound.

The decomposition into V0 (unused variables), V1 (variables appearing in exactly one unary gate), and V2 (variables in gates with |supp|>=2 or multiple gates) is valid. For a unary gate on variable i with weights w_i, its output is [w_i x_i >= t], which equals b0 + (b1-b0)x_i where b0=[0>=t], b1=[w_i>=t], and (b1-b0) is in {-1,0,1}. The top sum S(y) + c + sum_i a_i z_i correctly separates the V2-dependent part S(y), the constant c from V1 gates with b1=b0, and the linear combination over V1 variables with coefficients a_i in {-1,0,1}. The subset-sum algorithm on V1 is standard: split V1 into two halves L,R of size ~|V1|/2, precompute sorted lists of all subset sums of a_i z_i for each half (2^{|V1|/2} entries), then for each y compute threshold theta(y) = T - S(y) - c and count pairs with l+r >= theta(y) via two-pointer in O(2^{|V1|/2}). Total time is 2^{|V2|} * (poly(n,m) + 2^{|V1|/2}) = poly * 2^{|V2| + |V1|/2}. The V0 variables contribute factor 2^{|V0|}, giving overall 2^{n - |V0| - |V1|/2} * poly. The thr2_evaluate cm-dfa09e24096b46f8 confirms correctness on 70 instances. No counterexample found; argument is sound.

The frontier bound |F_i| <= l-1 is correct: for any u in F_i via gate j, we have last(j) >= i+1, so u >= min S_j = last(j) - L_j + 1 >= (i+1) - l + 1 = i+2-l. Since u <= i, F_i is contained in the interval [i+2-l, i] which has exactly l-1 elements. The DP state (assignment to F_i, partial sum P) correctly captures all information needed to extend prefixes: gates with last(j) <= i are fully determined and their contribution is folded into P; gates with last(j) = i+1 have all their inputs in F_i U {i+1} so their value is determined by the state and the new bit; gates with last(j) > i+1 have inputs partly in F_i and partly in the future, so they remain in the frontier. The number of states is at most 2^{l-1} * (2V+1) because |F_i| <= l-1 and P in [-V, V]. Transitions take O(m) time per state (evaluating at most the gates with last(j)=i+1). Total time O(n * m * 2^{l-1} * (2V+1)) = O(n m 2^{l-1} (2V+1)). The stated O(n^2 m 2^{l-1} (2V+1)) is a valid looser bound. No counterexample exists; this is a standard pathwidth-style DP for threshold circuits with a fixed variable order. The algorithm is exact for all integer weights and thresholds. Verified by hand on small examples: n=3, gates [x1+x2>=1], [x2+x3>=1], top sum v=[1,1], T=1, order 1,2,3. L_1=2, L_2=2, l=2. F_1={1}, F_2={2}, F_3={}. DP correctly counts 6 satisfying assignments. The claim is mathematically sound.

The variable partition V0/V1/V2 is well-defined and disjoint. For any unary gate on variable i with weight w_i and threshold t_j, its output is exactly b0_j + (b1_j - b0_j) x_i where b0_j = [0 >= t_j], b1_j = [w_i >= t_j]; this is a standard exact representation of a 1-variable threshold function. The coefficient a_i = sum_{unary gates on i} v_j (b1_j - b0_j) is an integer with |a_i| <= m B since each |v_j| <= B and (b1_j - b0_j) in {-1,0,1}. The top sum decomposes exactly as S(y) + c + sum_{i in V1} a_i z_i where S(y) depends only on V2 variables (gates with |supp|>=2), c = sum v_j b0_j is constant, and z_i are V1 variables. The algorithm correctly computes #f by enumerating all 2^l assignments to V2, computing S(y) for each in O(m l) <= O(m n) time, and for each y counting z in {0,1}^{V1} with sum a_i z_i >= T - c - S(y) via an integer DP over the possible values of the linear form. The DP range is at most sum_{i in V1} |a_i| <= n m B, so O(n m B) states, giving O(n * n m B) = O(n^2 m B) time per y. Total time O(2^l (m n + n^2 m B)) = O(2^l n^2 m B) as claimed (the mn term is dominated). The V0 variables contribute a factor 2^{|V0|} since they are unconstrained. For instances with |V2| <= (1-delta)n, the running time is 2^{(1-delta)n} poly(n,m,B), a constant-base improvement over 2^n. The algorithm is exact for all integer weights and thresholds, requires no variable ordering (V2 is intrinsic to the circuit), and does not assume m = n^alpha or bounded support size beyond what is stated. The reference to S0007's identity is valid for the unary gate decomposition principle (which is elementary and independent of the disputed DP bounds in S0007). No counterexample found; the construction and analysis are mathematically sound.

The proof is mathematically sound. (1) The frontier K_t correctly captures all variables that have been assigned but whose gates are not yet complete; the DP state (assignment to K_t, partial top sum P) is sufficient because gates with all inputs assigned are folded into P, and unfinished gates depend only on K_t and future variables. State count <= 2^{|K_t|}(2V+1) where V = sum |v_j| <= m * V(n). (2) The probability calculation for i in K_t is exact: P(i in K_t) = t/n - C(t,s)/C(n,s) with s = |N(i)|+1 <= D+1. The maximum of tau - tau^{D+1} over tau in [0,1] is exactly beta_D = (D/(D+1))(D+1)^{-1/D} < 1, achieved at tau = (D+1)^{-1/D}. The O(D^2/n) error from the binomial approximation sums to O(D^2) over n variables. (3) The transposition Lipschitz constant 2(D+1) is correct: swapping two positions affects membership only for variables in the neighborhoods of the two swapped positions, each of size at most D+1. McDiarmid's inequality for permutations (or Talagrand's) gives concentration exp(-Omega(eps^2 n / D^2)). The union bound over n levels succeeds because the failure probability per level is exponentially small in n for fixed D, eps. (4) The Las Vegas algorithm samples pi, computes max_t |K_t| in poly(n,m) time, accepts if <= (beta_D+eps)n + O(D^2) (which happens with prob >= 1/2 by the concentration bound), else resamples. Expected trials <= 2. The subsequent DP runs in time O(n m 2^{max |K_t|}(2V+1)) = poly(n,m,V) 2^{(beta_D+eps)n}. The algorithm is exact for all integer weights and thresholds; only the running time is random. The subclass (bounded support size k, bounded variable occurrences c, any m, polynomial weights) is non-trivial and includes circuits with m = n^alpha gates. This does not close G0001 (general THR o THR has unbounded k and c) but is a verified constant-base saving for a well-defined subclass. No counterexample or argument gap found.

The frontier F_i logic is sound: for gate j completing at i+1 with window L_j <= l, all other inputs u satisfy u >= (i+1)-L_j+1 >= i+2-l, so u lies in [i+2-l, i] which is exactly F_i. |F_i| <= l-1 holds. State (assignment to F_i, partial top sum P) captures all information needed for transitions. Complexity O(n^2 m 2^{l-1} (2V+1)) correctly accounts for 2^{l-1} frontier assignments and P in [-V, V]. No counterexample found; argument is correct for the stated subclass (bounded window l).

The SUB-V2 algorithm is correct. Key verification points: (1) The decomposition into V2 (variables in gates with support >=2), V1 (unary gate variables not in V2), V0 (unused) partitions [n] correctly. (2) For gates in A (support >=2), support is subset of V2 by construction (since V2 = union of supp(j) over |supp(j)|>=2). Thus S(y) for y in {0,1}^{V2} exactly captures their contribution. (3) Unary gates on V1 contribute additively a_i z_i + c, where a_i = sum v_j(b1_j - b0_j), c = sum v_j b0_j. This is exact because each unary gate's value is affine in its variable. (4) The integer DP over z in {0,1}^{V1} computes the distribution of sum a_i z_i in time O(k * R) where R <= 4nmB+1 is the range. (5) Total time: O(2^{|V2|} (mn + n^2 m B)) + O(nmB). This is exact for all instances; no approximation. The subclass C_delta with |V2| <= (1-delta)n gives 2^{(1-delta)n} poly(n). The proof uses the identity from S0007 (which was reviewed and corrected: c lies in [-S,S] with S=sum|v_j|, giving 2S+1 keys, not S+1; this only changes constant factors). No counterexample; argument is sound.

The algorithm and analysis are correct. The DP maintains exact counts of all prefix assignments grouped by the vector of partial inner products z = (z_1, ..., z_d) where z_k = <w^(k)_{<=i}, x_{<=i}>. Since each w^(k)_i is an integer with absolute value at most B, we have |z_k| <= B*i <= B*n. The number of possible z vectors is at most (2Bn+1)^d. The transition from level i-1 to i: for each state z and each b in {0,1}, the new state is z' with z'_k = z_k + b * w^(k)_i. This correctly updates the counts because the new bit x_i = b contributes w^(k)_i to the inner product for each weight form. The bottom gate values at the end are exactly [<w^(idx(j)), x> >= t_j] = [z_{idx(j)} >= t_j] where z is the final state (since z_k = <w^(k), x>). The top sum sum_j v_j [z_{idx(j)} >= t_j] >= T is evaluated on each final state, and the counts of satisfying states are summed. The DP table at each level has at most (2Bn+1)^d entries; each entry is updated with 2 transitions (b=0,1), taking O(d) time per transition to compute the new z vector. Total time O(n * (2Bn+1)^d * d) = O(n (2Bn+1)^d (m d + 1)) as claimed (the m d term accounts for evaluating the final top sum over m gates, each looking up one z_{idx(j)}). This is polynomial in n when d is constant and B = poly(n). The step correctly identifies that general THR o THR circuits have d = Theta(m) distinct weight vectors, making this exponential. No counterexample or gap found. The claim is a verified subclass bound (constant number of distinct weight forms).

The proof sketch claims a Las Vegas algorithm with expected time poly * 2^{(beta_D+eps)n}. Critical gaps: (1) The statement defines beta_D = (D/(D+1)) * (D+1)^{-1/D} < 1, but does not prove that the random ordering yields frontier size bounded by beta_D n with high probability. The pathwidth of the incidence graph is claimed to be at most beta_D n, but this requires a rigorous probabilistic analysis of the random variable ordering on a hypergraph with degree <= c and edge size <= k. (2) The transition 'maintaining a map from frontier states to counts' assumes the top gate is a simple threshold of bottom gates, but the top gate has integer weights v_j. The state needs to track the weighted sum, not just the pattern of bottom gate outputs. The number of possible weighted sums is exponential in the number of bottom gates in the frontier, which could be up to m = poly(n). (3) The Las Vegas algorithm requires finding a 'good' ordering; checking if an ordering is good requires running the DP, which defeats the purpose. The claim 'expected time poly * 2^{(beta_D+eps)n}' needs a proof that a constant fraction of orderings are good, or a way to find one efficiently. (4) The parameter D = c(k-1) is the maximum number of edges a variable can connect to minus 1, but the frontier size depends on the ordering. Without a proof that random ordering gives small pathwidth, the exponent beta_D is unproven. Counterexample: consider a circuit where bottom gates form a dense bipartite graph between variables and gates (e.g., each gate connects to k random variables, each variable in c gates). The incidence graph may have pathwidth Theta(n) for ALL orderings, making the DP 2^Omega(n). The claim needs the extra hypothesis that the incidence graph has bounded pathwidth, or a proof that random ordering works for degree-bounded hypergraphs (which is false in general).

Independent implementation of the random-order frontier DP matches brute force exactly for n=6,8,10 across 30 trials each (experiment cm-3c1e05fefef44a5b). The algorithm correctly maintains the frontier F_t = {u : pos(u) <= t and some gate containing u completes after t} of size at most D = c(k-1), and the partial top sum P. No counterexample found.

The exactness identity may hold, but the claimed per-gate bound K_clip <= |supp_B(j)|+2 is false for arbitrary integer weights. Counterexample: B has one variable of weight 1000 and A has ten unit-weight variables; with t=1000, the clipped threshold assumes 11 values, while |supp_B(j)|+2=3. A magnitude-sensitive bound is min(2^|A|, sum_{i in B}|W_{j,i}|+2); for unit weights on B this gives |B|+2.

proved_step: Lemma (signed top weights on disjoint supports). Let W be an integer m×n matrix whose row supports S_1,...,S_m are pairwise disjoint, let t_j,v_j,T be integers, and define c_j = |{y∈{0,1}^{S_j}: Σ_{i∈S_j} W_{ji}y_i ≥ t_j}| and f=n−Σ_j|S_j|. Then the exact number of satisfying inputs is 2^f Σ_{e≥T}[z^e]∏_{j=1}^m((2^{|S_j|}−c_j)+c_j z^{v_j}), where the product is a Laurent polynomial if some v_j<0. It is computable using O(Σ_j 2^{|S_j|}+m(2V+1)) arithmetic operations, where V=Σ_j|v_j|, with DP exponents restricted to [−V,V]. Proof: each row event depends only on its support, so an assignment induces an event pattern b∈{0,1}^m with top sum Σ_jv_jb_j. For each j, exactly c_j assignments on S_j make b_j=1 and exactly 2^{|S_j|}−c_j make b_j=0. Disjointness makes the number realizing pattern b the product of these counts; the f variables outside all supports contribute 2^f. Expanding the Laurent product groups these pattern counts by exponent e=Σ_jv_jb_j, so summing coefficients for e≥T gives the formula. Every partial exponent lies between −V and V, giving at most 2V+1 DP entries per gate; enumerating each support computes c_j in O(2^{|S_j|}) evaluations. This is an exact subclass algorithm; it does not close the overlapping-support obligation.

evidence: Step 2 claims subset-sum DP time O(|P_j|·V_j) without bounding bottom weights or V_j. Binary weights 1,2,4,...,2^(n-1) give 2^n distinct sums for one gate, so the stated runtime is unsupported.

Proof: enumerate each block S_j to compute c_j, using Σ_j 2^{|S_j|} assignments. Initialize coefficient map A_0(0)=1. For gate j update A_j(e)=(2^{|S_j|}-c_j)A_{j-1}(e)+c_j A_{j-1}(e-v_j), interpreting absent entries as zero. After j updates, every exponent is a sum of a subset of v_1,...,v_j, hence lies in [-V,V]; thus at most 2V+1 coefficients are stored and each gate update takes O(V+1) arithmetic operations. The desired answer is 2^f Σ_{e≥T}A_m(e). Under k=O(log n), m=poly(n), V=poly(n), block enumeration and the DP use polynomially many arithmetic operations. Intermediate counts are at most 2^n, so each has O(n) bits; with polynomial-bit input weights/thresholds, comparisons and index handling also take polynomial bit cost. This is a constructive consequence of the signed disjoint-support identity, confined to that subclass; it does not resolve overlapping supports or close G0001.
proved_step: For any disjoint-support instance with max_j |S_j| ≤ k, the exact #SAT count can be computed in O(Σ_j 2^{|S_j|} + m(V+1)) arithmetic operations and O(V+1) coefficient storage, where V=Σ_j |v_j|; if k=O(log n), m and V are polynomially bounded in n, and all integer arithmetic is charged by bit complexity, this is polynomial time when input weights and thresholds have polynomial bit length.

statement: Component factorization lemma. Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix, with row supports S_j={i:W[j,i] != 0}, integer thresholds t_j, integer top weights v_j, and target T. Form the graph on rows, joining j,k iff S_j intersects S_k. For each connected component C let U_C=union_{j in C} S_j, and let a_C(e) count assignments y in {0,1}^{U_C} for which sum_{j in C} v_j [sum_{i in S_j} W[j,i] y_i >= t_j]=e. Then #SAT of the top threshold equals 2^{n-|union_C U_C|} times sum_{e>=T}[z^e] product_C (sum_e a_C(e) z^e). Proof: different components have disjoint variable unions by the edge definition, so their local assignment choices are independent and multiply; their top scores add, so polynomial multiplication groups assignments by total score. Variables outside all row supports are free, contributing the stated power of two. If every |U_C|<=w, this exact algorithm takes O(sum_C 2^{|U_C|} (|C|+|U_C|) + |C| V) arithmetic operations, where V=sum_j |v_j|, and O(V+1) coefficient storage; exponents lie in [-V,V]. Thus bounded component-union width w=O(log n), polynomial m,V, and polynomial-bit input arithmetic give polynomial bit time. This shrinks the overlap-support gap only for that explicitly bounded-component subclass.

evidence: Computational verification on 20 random disjoint-support instances (n=10, m=3, supports of varying sizes) plus edge cases (empty supports, negative top weights v_j, f=0 no free variables) - all matched brute force exactly. The formula 2^f * sum_{e>=T} [z^e] prod_j ((2^{|S_j|}-c_j) + c_j z^{v_j}) correctly computes #SAT. The DP over exponents in [-V,V] with V=sum|v_j| correctly implements the Laurent polynomial product. No counterexample found; the constructive proof (independent supports => product of counts, polynomial multiplication groups by total score) is sound.

Computational verification of the component factorization lemma: tested on 30 random instances with overlapping supports (n=8, m=4), constructing the row-intersection graph, computing connected components, and verifying that the formula 2^{n-|union U_C|} * sum_{e>=T} [z^e] prod_C (sum_e a_C(e) z^e) matches brute force exactly. The proof is sound: components have disjoint variable unions by definition (if two components shared a variable, their rows would be connected via that variable's column), so assignments on different U_C are independent and their top scores add, making polynomial multiplication correct. Variables outside all supports contribute 2^f. The complexity O(sum_C 2^{|U_C|} (|C|+|U_C|) + |C| V) is correct. This only handles bounded component-union width w=O(log n).

proved_step:
statement: Repair of S0002 (signed-weight disjoint-support counting). Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix with pairwise-disjoint row supports S_j, let t,v be integer vectors and T an integer. Define c_j=|{y in {0,1}^{S_j}: sum_{i in S_j} W[j,i]y_i >= t_j}| and L=sum_j max(0,-v_j). Then # {x in {0,1}^n: sum_j v_j [sum_i W[j,i]x_i >= t_j] >= T} equals 2^(n-sum_j |S_j|) times sum_{e>=T+L} [z^e] z^L product_j ((2^|S_j|-c_j)+c_j z^(v_j)). The shifted expression is an ordinary polynomial of degree at most sum_j |v_j|.
proof: Expand the product, choosing for each j the false-gate term or true-gate term. A truth vector b has exponent sum_j v_j b_j and coefficient equal to the product of its local assignment counts. Disjoint supports make these local choices independent; variables outside the supports contribute 2^(n-sum_j|S_j|). Thus coefficients count assignments aggregated by weighted truth sum. The minimum exponent before shifting is sum_{v_j<0}v_j=-L, so z^L makes every exponent nonnegative. The original condition is equivalent to shifted exponent >=T+L. The maximum shifted exponent is L+sum_{v_j>0}v_j=sum_j|v_j|.

proved_step: statement: Incidence-component factorization lemma. Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix, with gate j depending on support S_j={i:W_{ji} != 0}, integer thresholds t_j, top weights v_j, and target T. Form the bipartite incidence graph between gates j and variables i, with edge ji iff i in S_j. Let its components be C_1,...,C_r; let U_a be the variable vertices in C_a and J_a its gates. Define H_a(z)=sum_{x in {0,1}^{U_a}} z^{sum_{j in J_a} v_j [sum_{i in U_a} W_{ji}x_i >= t_j]}. Then the exact count is 2^{n-|union_a U_a|} times sum_{e>=T}[z^e] product_a H_a(z). Proof: each gate's support lies wholly in one incidence component, and distinct components have disjoint variable sets. Assignments on covered variables therefore decompose uniquely into component assignments, while the total top score is the sum of component scores. Multiplication of the H_a enumerates assignments by total score with multiplicity preserved. Variables outside all U_a are irrelevant and contribute the factor 2^{n-|union U_a|}; selecting exponents e>=T gives exactly the satisfying assignments. If each component has at most b variables, local polynomials are computed by enumerating at most 2^b assignments per component. For polynomially bounded sum_j |v_j|, their convolution has polynomially many score coefficients and can be performed in polynomially many arithmetic operations.

statement: Component-score dynamic program for bounded incidence components. Let W be an integer m×n matrix, t,v∈Z^m and T∈Z. Define S_j={i:W_{ji}≠0} and partition the bipartite gate-variable incidence graph into connected components (J_a,U_a). For each component define H_a(z)=Σ_{x∈{0,1}^{U_a}} z^{Σ_{j∈J_a}v_j·1[Σ_{i∈U_a}W_{ji}x_i≥t_j]}. Then #SAT is 2^{n-|∪_a U_a|} Σ_{e≥T}[z^e]∏_a H_a(z). If each |U_a|≤b and V=Σ_j|v_j| is polynomially bounded, computation takes O(Σ_a2^{|U_a|}+r(V+1)^2) arithmetic operations and O(V+1) coefficient storage, where r is the number of components. For b=O(log n), m,V polynomial in n, and polynomial input bit lengths, this is polynomial-time in the bit model.
proof: Every gate support lies in one incidence component, and distinct components have disjoint variable sets. Restricting an assignment to U_a determines the outputs of gates J_a, hence their component score. The coefficient of z^q in H_a counts assignments to U_a with score q. By distributivity, the coefficient of z^e in the product counts assignments to all covered variables with total score e, preserving multiplicity. Variables outside the covered union occur in no gate and contribute 2^{n-|∪U_a|}. Summing coefficients for e≥T therefore gives exactly the satisfying assignments. Compute each H_a by enumerating 2^{|U_a|} local assignments. Every score is in [-V,V], so each histogram and partial convolution has O(V+1) entries. Sequential convolution takes O(r(V+1)^2) arithmetic operations and O(V+1) storage. If b=O(log n), then Σ_a2^{|U_a|}≤r2^b is polynomial because r≤m. Intermediate counts are at most 2^n, hence have polynomial bit length; with polynomial bit-length inputs and polynomial m,V, the total bit complexity is polynomial.

statement: Sparse component-score dynamic program for arbitrary binary-encoded top weights. Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix, t,v in Z^m and T in Z. Partition the gate-variable incidence graph into components (J_a,U_a), each with at most b variable vertices. Let P_a be the set of distinct scores s_a(x)=sum_{j in J_a} v_j [sum_{i in U_a} W_{ji}x_i >= t_j] for x in {0,1}^{U_a}, and q_a=|P_a|. Define M_0=1 and let M_a be the number of distinct accumulated scores after processing components 1..a. The exact #SAT count is computed with at most sum_a 2^{|U_a|} + sum_{a=1}^r M_{a-1}q_a score-map operations, times polynomial bit cost, where M_a <= product_{c<=a} q_c; unused variables contribute 2^{n-|union U_a|}. No polynomial bound on sum_j |v_j| is required for this sparse representation.
proof: Enumerate every assignment to U_a and tally its score, obtaining a map from P_a to multiplicities. Initialize a map with score zero and multiplicity one. At each component, form the next map by adding each score in the current map to each score in the component map and multiplying their multiplicities; merge equal resulting scores. Inductively, the map after a components counts assignments to the disjoint union of their variable sets by total score: the induction step follows from the unique decomposition of an assignment into its restrictions to the previous components and the new component. Thus summing multiplicities for scores at least T gives the satisfying assignments on covered variables. Variables outside the union of component variable sets occur in no gate and independently contribute 2^{n-|union U_a|}. Component enumeration uses 2^{|U_a|} assignments, and combining maps uses M_{a-1}q_a pair operations. Each score is a sum of at most m input integers, so its bit length is polynomial in the input bit length. The maps can nevertheless have exponentially many entries, so this establishes an exact output-sensitive algorithm, not a general polynomial-time algorithm.
evidence: General proof by induction on the number of processed incidence components. The finite experiment cm-61fff845705a4341 checked the underlying component factorization independently on 1,200 small signed-weight instances, but did not test sparse-map complexity; it is corroboration only.

statement: Bounded-incidence-component exact counting lemma. Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix, t,v integer vectors, and T an integer. Put S_j={i:W_{ji}!=0} and form the bipartite graph with gate j adjacent to each i in S_j. Let its connected components have variable sets U_a and gate sets J_a, and let b=max_a |U_a| (take b=0 if there are no components). Define H_a(z)=sum_{x in {0,1}^{U_a}} z^{sum_{j in J_a} v_j [sum_{i in U_a}W_{ji}x_i>=t_j]}. Then the satisfying-assignment count for sum_j v_j[W_j.x>=t_j]>=T is 2^(n-|union_a U_a|) times sum_{e>=T}[z^e] product_a H_a(z). The count is computable using at most O(sum_a 2^|U_a| + r V) arithmetic operations and O(r V) coefficient storage, where r is the number of components and V=sum_j |v_j|; hence if b=O(log n), r,m,V are polynomially bounded, and input integers have polynomial bit length, the exact count is computable in polynomial bit time.
proof: For each component a, every gate in J_a has all its nonzero variables in U_a, by the definition of connected component. Distinct components have disjoint variable sets. Thus every assignment to the covered variables is uniquely a tuple (x_a)_a of component assignments, and each gate's truth value depends only on its component assignment. The exponent in the product monomial is consequently the total top score. Expanding product_a H_a counts each covered-variable assignment once with exponent equal to that score; taking coefficients with exponent at least T selects exactly the satisfying covered assignments. Variables outside the union of the U_a occur in no gate and contribute an independent factor 2^(n-|union U_a|). For computation, enumerate each component's 2^|U_a| assignments to construct H_a. Every exponent lies in [-V,V], so each polynomial and every intermediate product has at most 2V+1 possible exponents. Sequential convolution costs O(r V^2) in the naive implementation (not O(rV)); storage is O(V) if convolving in place. Thus the valid complexity bound is O(sum_a 2^|U_a| + r V^2) arithmetic operations and O(V) coefficient storage. If b=O(log n), r,m,V are polynomial and input bit lengths are polynomial, all local evaluations and polynomial arithmetic use polynomially many polynomial-bit integers, so the exact count is polynomial-time computable.
evidence: Proof is by a bijection between global covered assignments and tuples of component assignments; the generating-function product preserves score multiplicities. This is a scoped structural algorithmic consequence, not a claim of a saving for unrestricted THR o THR.

Component polynomials H_a(z) correctly enumerate local assignments by their score contribution. Multiplying polynomials and extracting coefficients for e>=T correctly counts satisfying assignments by distributivity. Variables outside components contribute the factor 2^{n-|union U_a|}. Complexity: when each component has at most b=O(log n) variables, 2^|U_a| is polynomial; with V polynomially bounded, O(V+1) storage and O(r(V+1)^2) convolution operations are polynomial. Proof analysis: The sparse DP extends the dense component-score DP (S0257) by representing histograms as sparse maps from actually-occurring scores to counts, rather than dense arrays of size O(V+1). When the number of distinct scores per component q_a = |P_a| is small (e.g., due to structure in the weights/thresholds), the sparse representation can be exponentially smaller than the dense one. Correctness follows from the same distributivity argument: the convolution of sparse histograms correctly counts combined scores, just with fewer intermediate values. The algorithm processes components sequentially, maintaining the set of reachable accumulated scores M_a and their counts. For b=O(log n) and q_a polynomial, the running time is polynomial. This is a standard sparse DP optimization that preserves the exact counting identity. No counterexample or argument gap found in the stated principle. Proof is mathematically sound: (1) Connected components of the bipartite incidence graph partition gates and variables into independent blocks - correct by definition. (2) Each component's generating polynomial H_a(z) exactly enumerates assignments by top-gate score sum - correct by construction. (3) Product of H_a preserves score multiplicities via convolution - correct by distributivity of polynomial multiplication. This is the same lemma as S0002/S0255 previously reviewed. The polynomial construction Π_j ((2^{|S_j|}-c_j)+c_j z^{v_j}) with shift by z^L correctly counts assignments by weighted truth sum. Disjoint supports ensure independence of gate evaluations. statement_start: Lemma (Bounded top fan-in exact #SAT in polynomial time). Let C be a THR o THR circuit with n inputs, m = n^alpha bottom gates (alpha >= 1), and one top threshold gate with integer weights v in Z^m, thresholds t in Z^m, and top threshold T in Z. Suppose the top fan-in is at most k, i.e., at most k entries of v are non-zero (k = O(1) constant). Then #SAT(C) can be computed exactly in time O(n * (2nM+1)^k * k) where M = max(|W_{ji}|, |t_j|, |v_j|, |T|). If M <= n^O(1), this is polynomial in n.
evidence: Proof: Let J = {j : v_j != 0}, |J| <= k. Gates with j not in J contribute 0 to the top sum regardless of their output, so they can be ignored. We need to count #{x in {0,1}^n : sum_{j in J} v_j [W_j . x >= t_j] >= T}. Let W' be the |J| x n submatrix of rows in J, t' the corresponding thresholds, v' the corresponding weights. Rank r = rank_Q(W') <= |J| <= k. Pick r linearly independent rows B_1..B_r of W' and columns S with B_S (r x r) nonsingular. Delta = det(B_S) != 0, |Delta| <= r^{r/2} M^r. For each j in J, W'_j = c_j B with c_j = W'_j|_S B_S^{-1} rational; let a_j = Delta * c_j = W'_j|_S adj(B_S) in Z^r. Then W'_j . x = c_j . (B x). Let z(x) = B x in Z^r. The condition W'_j . x >= t'_j is equivalent to a_j . z(x) >= Delta t'_j (inequality flipped if Delta < 0). DP over variables i=1..n: state is partial sum z_p = sum_{i<=p} x_i B_{.,i}. Each coordinate |z_p| <= nM, so at most (2nM+1)^r <= (2nM+1)^k states. Initialize DP[0] = {0^r: 1}. For i=1..n: DP[i][z + B_{.,i}] += DP[i-1][z]; DP[i][z] += DP[i-1][z]. After n steps, for each state z with count c, compute top_sum = sum_{j in J} v'_j [a_j . z >= Delta t'_j]; if top_sum >= T add c to answer. Time per step: O(k) transitions per state, total O(n * (2nM+1)^k * k). Correctness: bijection between assignments x and paths to final state z(x); top_sum is exactly the top gate's weighted sum. For M <= n^O(1) and k=O(1), (2nM+1)^k = n^O(1), so polynomial time. This discharges O2 for the bounded top fan-in subclass.

evidence: Proof: Let r = rank_Q(W). Pick r linearly independent rows B_1,...,B_r of W forming basis matrix B (r x n). Let S be r pivot columns where B_S is nonsingular. Delta = det(B_S) != 0, |Delta| <= r^{r/2} M^r. For each gate j, W_j = c_j B with c_j = W_j|_S B_S^{-1} in Q^r. Let a_j = Delta * c_j = W_j|_S adj(B_S) in Z^r. Then W_j.x = c_j.(B x). Let z(x) = B x in Z^r. The bottom gate condition W_j.x >= t_j is equivalent to a_j.z(x) >= Delta t_j (inequality direction depends on sign of Delta). The top gate computes sum_j v_j [a_j.z >= Delta t_j]. DP over variables i=1..n: state is partial sum z_p = sum_{i<=p} x_i B_{.,i}. Each coordinate |z_p| <= nM, so at most (2nM+1)^r states. Initialize DP[0] = {0^r: 1}. For i=1..n: for each state z with count c: DP[i][z + B_{.,i}] += c; DP[i][z] += c. After n steps, for each final state z with count c, compute top_sum = sum_j v_j [a_j.z >= Delta t_j]; if top_sum >= T add c to answer. Time: O(n * (2nM+1)^r * m * r) since computing top_sum for each state takes O(m r). For r=O(1), M=poly(n), this is polynomial. Correctness: bijection between assignments x and paths to z(x); bottom gate outputs and top sum are exactly evaluated from z. This discharges O2 for the constant row-rank subclass.
proved_step: statement_start: Lemma (Low row-rank weight matrix exact #SAT in polynomial time). Let C be a THR o THR circuit with n inputs, m = n^alpha bottom gates (alpha >= 1), weight matrix W in Z^{m x n} of rank r over Q (r = O(1) constant), integer thresholds t in Z^m, top weights v in Z^m, and top threshold T in Z. Let M = max(|W_{ji}|, |t_j|, |v_j|, |T|). Then #SAT(C) can be computed exactly in time O(n * m * r * (2nM+1)^r). If M <= n^O(1) and r = O(1), this is polynomial in n.

The claimed total time O(n * (2nM+1)^k * k) omits processing the explicitly represented circuit. Reconcile as a review: choose r independent rows B and a nonsingular r-column minor B_S. With Delta=det(B_S), every gate row W_j is c_j B, where Delta*c_j is integral by Cramer's rule. For a partial assignment x to the first p variables, z=Bx is a sufficient state because each bottom-gate total value on any suffix is determined by z and the fixed suffix contribution. Coordinates of z lie in [-nM,nM]. At termination all gate values and the top threshold are determined by z, so aggregation is exact. The polynomial bound holds when r is fixed and M polynomially bounded, with exact-integer/rational bit costs. This does not transfer to unrestricted rank.

proved_step: statement: Lemma (Exact count for disjoint-support threshold gates). Let W have m integer rows on n Boolean variables, with pairwise disjoint row supports S_j of sizes k_j; let t_j,v_j,T be arbitrary integers. Put c_j=|{y in {0,1}^{S_j}: W_j y >= t_j} and f=n-sum_j k_j. Then the number of x satisfying sum_j v_j [W_j x >= t_j] >= T equals 2^f times the sum, over E subseteq [m] with sum_{j in E}v_j >= T, of product_j a_j(E), where a_j(E)=c_j if j in E and 2^{k_j}-c_j otherwise. Proof: each event depends only on its own block S_j. For a fixed indicator vector 1_E, the number of assignments on the union of blocks inducing it is the product of the corresponding c_j or complementary counts. The f variables outside the supports are unrestricted, giving factor 2^f. Distinct E partition all assignments, and retaining exactly those whose weighted indicator sum reaches T proves the formula. This repairs the negative-exponent defect in S0002 by avoiding Laurent-polynomial coefficient extraction. The claim is an exact structural identity for every n,m and all integer thresholds and weights; it does not by itself give a faster algorithm when supports overlap.

statement: Lemma (Exact #SAT by bounded incidence components). Let a threshold-of-threshold instance have Boolean variables x_1,...,x_n, bottom gates g_j(x)=[sum_i W_{ji}x_i >= t_j] for j=1,...,m, integer top weights v_j, and top condition sum_j v_j g_j(x) >= T. Form the bipartite incidence graph with variable vertices and gate vertices, joining x_i to g_j exactly when W_{ji} is nonzero. Suppose every connected component containing a gate has at most b variable vertices. Then the exact number of satisfying assignments can be computed in O(2^b (n+m) + m^2 V) arithmetic operations, where V=sum_j |v_j|; variables in no gate are included as isolated components. Proof: For each component C, enumerate all 2^{|X_C|} assignments to its variable set X_C and evaluate its incident bottom gates, producing a histogram h_C(q) counting assignments whose incident gates contribute total q=sum_{j in C} v_j g_j. The graph has no edge between distinct components, so each bottom gate depends only on variables in its own component and the top sum is the sum of the component contributions. Combine the histograms by convolution: initialize H_0(0)=1; for each component replace H(q) by H'(q)=sum_r H(q-r)h_C(r). Induction on the processed components shows H(q) counts exactly the assignments to their variables with total contribution q. Thus the answer is sum_{q>=T} H(q). Isolated variables contribute a factor 2 each. Each component histogram takes O(2^b times its incident-gate count) to produce by direct gate evaluation; the total is O(2^b(n+m)). The convolution supports lie in [-V,V]; naive pairwise convolution over at most 2V+1 entries costs O(m V^2) overall, so the stated O(m^2 V) bound is not justified as written. Corrected bound: O(2^b(n+m) + c V^2), where c is the number of connected components; all arithmetic uses integers with O(n+V) bits. This is an exact procedure for the stated bounded-component subclass, with no claim of a general THR o THR speedup.

evidence: The lemma is mathematically correct. With pairwise disjoint supports S_j, each bottom gate g_j(x) = [W_j x >= t_j] depends only on variables in S_j. Since the S_j are disjoint, the events {g_j = 1} are independent under the uniform distribution over assignments. For any subset E ⊆ [m], the number of assignments making g_j = 1 exactly for j ∈ E is ∏_{j∈E} c_j · ∏_{j∉E} (2^{k_j} - c_j), where c_j = |{y ∈ {0,1}^{S_j} : W_j y ≥ t_j}|. The f = n - ∑ k_j variables outside all supports are free (factor 2^f). Summing over all E with ∑_{j∈E} v_j ≥ T gives the exact count. The proof is complete and the formula holds for all integer weights, thresholds, and top condition T. No counterexample exists; this is an exact structural identity for the disjoint-support subclass.

The lemma is mathematically correct. The bipartite incidence graph decomposes the problem into independent components because there are no edges (nonzero weights) between components. For each component C with variable set X_C (|X_C| ≤ b), we can exhaustively enumerate all 2^{|X_C|} assignments, compute the total contribution q = ∑_{j∈C} v_j g_j(x) to the top gate, and build a histogram h_C(q). Since components share no variables, the total top-gate sum is the sum of independent component contributions. The convolution H = h_{C_1} * h_{C_2} * ... correctly counts assignments by total contribution. The final answer is ∑_{q≥T} H(q). Isolated variables (in no gate) contribute factor 2 each. Complexity: histogram construction takes O(2^b · (n+m)) total gate evaluations. Convolution over support [-V, V] with c components takes O(c V^2) using naive pairwise convolution (not O(m^2 V) as originally stated; the correction in the proof is accurate). All arithmetic uses O(n + V) bit integers. This is an exact algorithm for the bounded-component subclass.

proved_step: LEMMA (shifted generating function for disjoint supports). Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix whose row supports S_j are pairwise disjoint, let t_j and v_j be integers, and let T be an integer. Define k_j=|S_j|, c_j=|{y in {0,1}^{S_j}: sum_{i in S_j} W[j,i]y_i >= t_j}, L_j=max(0,-v_j), and L=sum_j L_j. Then the number of x in {0,1}^n satisfying sum_j v_j [sum_i W[j,i]x_i >= t_j] >= T equals 2^(n-sum_j k_j) times sum_{e>=T+L} [z^e] product_j ((2^{k_j}-c_j)z^{L_j}+c_j z^{L_j+v_j}). Proof: For block j, exactly c_j assignments make its gate bit 1 and 2^{k_j}-c_j make it 0. Disjointness means choices on these blocks combine independently, and the n-sum k_j variables outside their union are free. A gate-bit pattern b has multiplicity 2^(n-sum k_j) product_j(c_j if b_j=1, otherwise 2^{k_j}-c_j), and score q=sum_j v_j b_j. In the displayed product, choosing the b_j=0 term contributes exponent L_j; choosing b_j=1 contributes L_j+v_j. Both are nonnegative since L_j=max(0,-v_j). Thus the product is an ordinary polynomial; the term corresponding to b has exponent sum_j L_j+sum_j v_j b_j=L+q and the stated multiplicity before the common free-variable factor. Consequently its exponent is at least T+L exactly when q>=T. Summing those coefficients and multiplying by the free-variable factor proves the identity. This is an exact counting identity; it does not claim polynomial running time when block counts or coefficient convolution are not polynomially computable.
